hook.text: Amazon found that every 100 milliseconds of latency cost them one percent in sales.

buildup.text: Google discovered that a half-second delay in search results dropped traffic by 20 percent.

discovery.text: Speed isn't a nice-to-have. It directly determines how much money a website makes.

twist.text: Users don't complain about slow sites. They just leave — silently and permanently.

climax.text: Performance is the invisible feature that makes or breaks every other feature on the page.

punchline.text: Speed is a feature users never notice until it's gone.

quiz.question: What did Amazon discover about latency?

hook.text: Humans perceive anything under 100 milliseconds as instant. Our brains can't detect it.

buildup.text: After one second, users notice the delay. After three seconds, they consider leaving.

discovery.text: Progress indicators trick the brain into patience. Spinners buy time that blank screens can't.

twist.text: Perceived performance matters more than actual speed. Skeleton screens feel faster than they are.

climax.text: Web performance is as much psychology as engineering — fool the brain and users stay.

punchline.text: Feeling fast matters more than being fast.

quiz.question: At what delay do users notice a page is slow?

topics.title: Mobile Speed and the Real World

hook.text: Most developers test on fast Wi-Fi. Most users browse on spotty 3G connections.

buildup.text: In emerging markets, a web page may take 20 seconds to load on average hardware.

discovery.text: Mobile devices have less RAM, slower CPUs, and unreliable networks than development machines.

twist.text: The next billion internet users will come from regions with the slowest connections.

climax.text: Building for the slowest device means building for the widest possible audience.

punchline.text: Your test environment is not your user's reality.

quiz.question: Why is mobile performance often worse than desktop?
options: Less RAM, slower CPUs, and weaker networks

hook.text: In 2010, Google announced page speed would affect search rankings. The web panicked.

buildup.text: Suddenly performance wasn't just about user experience — it affected discoverability.

discovery.text: Core Web Vitals in 2021 made specific performance metrics part of Google's ranking algorithm.

twist.text: Many sites that ranked first for years suddenly dropped because they loaded too slowly.

climax.text: Google turned performance into an SEO requirement, forcing the entire web to speed up.

punchline.text: Google made speed a ranking factor for everyone.

quiz.question: When did Google make page speed a ranking signal?

hook.text: Without limits, websites grow heavier every sprint. New features add kilobytes quietly.

buildup.text: A performance budget sets hard limits: no more than 200 KB of JavaScript, for example.

discovery.text: Teams with budgets catch regressions before users do. The budget becomes a quality gate.

twist.text: Most teams set budgets once and then ignore them under deadline pressure.

climax.text: The teams that enforce budgets ship faster sites year after year. Discipline beats talent.

punchline.text: What gets measured gets managed.

quiz.question: What does a performance budget limit?

hook.text: A browser must complete a series of steps before it can paint a single pixel on screen.

buildup.text: It downloads HTML, parses it, fetches CSS, builds the DOM and CSSOM, then calculates layout.

discovery.text: This chain of dependencies is called the critical rendering path. Each step blocks the next.

twist.text: One render-blocking CSS file can delay the entire page, even if the HTML arrived instantly.

climax.text: Optimizing the critical path means removing bottlenecks from this dependency chain.

punchline.text: First paint is a chain — break any link and it stalls.

quiz.question: What does the critical rendering path determine?
options: When the browser can first paint pixels
How long the server takes to respond

hook.text: CSS and synchronous scripts can freeze the entire rendering pipeline until they load.

buildup.text: The browser pauses painting when it encounters a stylesheet it hasn't downloaded yet.

discovery.text: Scripts without 'async' or 'defer' halt HTML parsing completely while they execute.

twist.text: A tiny analytics script in the head tag can delay your entire above-the-fold content.

climax.text: Identifying and eliminating render blockers is the fastest way to improve load time.

punchline.text: The fastest resource is the one you don't block on.

quiz.question: What can block the browser from rendering?

hook.text: A 200 KB image and 200 KB of JavaScript are not equally expensive for the browser.

buildup.text: Images just need decoding. JavaScript must be parsed, compiled, and executed line by line.

discovery.text: On a mid-range phone, parsing one megabyte of JavaScript can take over four seconds.

twist.text: Most websites ship megabytes of JavaScript that users never even trigger or interact with.

climax.text: JavaScript is the most expensive resource on the web, byte for byte, bar none.

punchline.text: Not all bytes cost the same to process.

quiz.question: Why is JavaScript more expensive than an image of the same size?
options: It must be parsed, compiled, and executed

hook.text: Why download a page's footer images before the user even scrolls past the hero?

buildup.text: Lazy loading delays non-critical resources until they're actually needed.

discovery.text: Code splitting breaks JavaScript into chunks loaded on demand, not all upfront.

twist.text: Native lazy loading landed in browsers in 2019. Before that, developers used JS libraries.

climax.text: Loading only what's needed, when it's needed, cuts initial page weight dramatically.

punchline.text: Don't load what the user hasn't asked for yet.

quiz.question: What does code splitting do?
options: Breaks JS into chunks loaded on demand

hook.text: Sometimes the browser discovers a critical resource too late in the loading process.

buildup.text: Preload hints tell the browser to start fetching a resource before it naturally discovers it.

discovery.text: Prefetch goes further — downloading resources the user will probably need on the next page.

twist.text: Overusing preload can backfire. Too many hints compete for bandwidth and slow everything down.

climax.text: Smart preloading is surgical — prioritize the one font or script that blocks first paint.

punchline.text: Hint wisely and the browser rewards you.

quiz.question: What does prefetch do?
options: Downloads resources for a likely next page

hook.text: When does a page feel loaded? Google says it's when the biggest visible element appears.

buildup.text: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures the time until the main image or text block renders.

discovery.text: A good LCP is under 2.5 seconds. Anything slower signals a poor user experience to Google.

twist.text: A huge hero image can tank your LCP if it loads from a slow server without optimization.

climax.text: LCP became the most important Core Web Vital for measuring perceived load speed.

punchline.text: The biggest element sets the pace for the page.

quiz.question: What does LCP measure?
options: Time until the largest element renders

hook.text: You're about to tap a button and suddenly the page jumps. An ad loaded above it.

buildup.text: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures how much page content moves unexpectedly during load.

discovery.text: A good CLS score is under 0.1. Anything higher means elements are shifting around too much.

twist.text: Images without width and height attributes are the number one cause of layout shift worldwide.

climax.text: CLS turned a user annoyance into a measurable metric that affects search rankings.

punchline.text: Set your dimensions or watch your content dance.

quiz.question: What causes high CLS scores?

hook.text: A page can load fast but feel sluggish when you try to interact with it.

buildup.text: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures the delay between a click and the visual response.

discovery.text: Good INP is under 200 milliseconds. Slower means the page feels unresponsive to touch.

twist.text: INP replaced First Input Delay in 2024 because it measures all interactions, not just the first.

climax.text: INP captures what users actually feel — whether the page responds when they act.

punchline.text: Responsiveness is the metric users feel most.

quiz.question: What replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital?

hook.text: Lighthouse says your site is fast. Real users say it's slow. Who's right?

buildup.text: Lab tools test on powerful machines with fast networks. Field data comes from real users.

discovery.text: Chrome User Experience Report collects real performance data from millions of Chrome users.

twist.text: A perfect Lighthouse score means nothing if real users on slow phones experience something else.

climax.text: Field data tells you what users actually experience. Lab data tells you what to fix.

punchline.text: Test in the lab; trust the field.

quiz.question: Why can lab data differ from field data?
options: Lab uses fast hardware, users don't

hook.text: Chrome DevTools includes a built-in performance auditor. It's called Lighthouse.

buildup.text: Lighthouse scores your page on performance, accessibility, SEO, and best practices.

discovery.text: It provides specific recommendations: compress images, remove unused JavaScript, defer CSS.

twist.text: Chasing a perfect 100 score can lead to diminishing returns. Real-world impact matters more.

climax.text: Lighthouse democratized performance testing. Any developer can audit a page in seconds.

punchline.text: One click shows you exactly what to fix.

quiz.question: What does Lighthouse measure?

hook.text: A server in Virginia takes 200 ms to reach a user in Tokyo. Physics sets the speed limit.

buildup.text: CDNs copy your content to servers worldwide. Users download from the nearest one.

discovery.text: Cloudflare, Akamai, and Fastly run edge servers in hundreds of cities across every continent.

twist.text: CDNs were once only for big companies. Now services like Vercel and Netlify CDN everything free.

climax.text: CDNs made geographic distance nearly irrelevant for static content delivery.

punchline.text: Copy it closer to beat the speed of light.

quiz.question: What do CDNs reduce?
options: Physical distance between user and content

hook.text: HTTP/1.1 loaded resources one at a time per connection. Six connections was the browser limit.

buildup.text: Developers hacked around this by combining files, using sprites, and sharding domains.

discovery.text: HTTP/2 introduced multiplexing — many resources flowing through one connection simultaneously.

twist.text: Many old optimization tricks like file concatenation actually hurt performance under HTTP/2.

climax.text: HTTP/2 made the network layer smarter so developers could stop working around its limits.

punchline.text: Better protocols made old hacks unnecessary.

quiz.question: What did HTTP/2 introduce?

hook.text: Images account for roughly half of all bytes transferred on an average web page.

buildup.text: Formats like JPEG, PNG, and GIF were designed decades ago without the modern web in mind.

discovery.text: WebP and AVIF compress images 30-50% smaller than JPEG with comparable visual quality.

twist.text: Many sites still serve unoptimized PNGs because no one checked the asset pipeline.

climax.text: Responsive images with srcset serve the right size to every screen, saving mobile users megabytes.

punchline.text: The easiest performance win is smaller images.

quiz.question: What percentage of page weight do images typically represent?

hook.text: The fastest HTTP request is the one that never happens. Caching makes that possible.

buildup.text: Cache-Control headers tell the browser how long to reuse a downloaded resource.

discovery.text: Immutable assets with content hashes can be cached forever — the filename changes when content does.

twist.text: Bad caching causes stale content bugs that are nearly impossible to debug from the server side.

climax.text: A solid caching strategy can eliminate 80% of requests on repeat visits.

punchline.text: Cache well and most requests disappear.

quiz.question: What can caching eliminate on repeat visits?

hook.text: Text-based files like HTML, CSS, and JavaScript shrink dramatically when compressed.

buildup.text: Gzip has been the default web compression for over two decades. It's fast and reliable.

discovery.text: Brotli, developed by Google, compresses 15-20% better than Gzip for text content.

twist.text: Brotli is slower to compress but faster to decompress. Pre-compressing at build time fixes this.

climax.text: Every modern browser supports Brotli. Free performance is sitting on most servers, unclaimed.

punchline.text: Compression is free speed hiding in plain sight.

quiz.question: How much better does Brotli compress than Gzip?

hook.text: After the browser builds the DOM and CSSOM, the real work of painting pixels begins.

buildup.text: The pipeline flows: style calculation, layout, paint, and finally compositing on the GPU.

discovery.text: Changing certain CSS properties triggers different stages. Some are cheap; others are expensive.

twist.text: Animating width or height forces layout recalculation. Animating transform skips to compositing.

climax.text: Knowing which properties trigger which pipeline stages is the key to smooth animations.

punchline.text: Animate the cheap properties; avoid the rest.

quiz.question: Which CSS property is cheapest to animate?

hook.text: Reading an element's size, then changing it, then reading again causes the browser to panic.

buildup.text: Each read forces the browser to recalculate layout. Rapid read-write loops multiply the cost.

discovery.text: This is called layout thrashing — it can drop frame rates from 60 fps to single digits.

twist.text: A single for-loop reading offsetHeight and setting style can freeze the page for seconds.

climax.text: Batching reads and writes separately prevents thrashing and keeps animations fluid.

punchline.text: Read all first, then write all. Never mix.

quiz.question: What causes layout thrashing?

hook.text: Most screens refresh 60 times per second. That gives JavaScript 16 milliseconds per frame.

buildup.text: If your code takes longer than 16 ms, the browser drops a frame. Users see jank.

discovery.text: requestAnimationFrame schedules work in sync with the display refresh for smooth rendering.

twist.text: Modern phones run at 120 Hz. That cuts the budget to just 8 milliseconds per frame.

climax.text: Hitting consistent frame rates requires treating every millisecond as precious.

punchline.text: Sixteen milliseconds is all you get per frame.

quiz.question: How much time does 60fps give per frame?

hook.text: JavaScript runs on a single thread. Heavy computation blocks rendering and user input.

buildup.text: Web Workers let you run scripts in background threads that don't block the main thread.

discovery.text: Complex calculations, data processing, and parsing can happen without freezing the interface.

twist.text: Workers can't touch the DOM directly. They communicate through messages, adding complexity.

climax.text: Moving work off the main thread is the only way to keep interactive responsiveness at scale.

punchline.text: Heavy work belongs in the background thread.

quiz.question: What limitation do Web Workers have?

hook.text: Modern browsers don't paint everything on one surface. They split content into layers.

buildup.text: The GPU composites these layers together, handling transforms and opacity at hardware speed.

discovery.text: Promoting an element to its own layer with 'will-change' lets the GPU animate it cheaply.

twist.text: Too many layers waste GPU memory. Mobile devices crash when layer count spirals out of control.

climax.text: Layer management is a balancing act between smooth animation and memory efficiency.

punchline.text: The GPU is powerful but not unlimited.

quiz.question: What hardware handles compositing layers?

hook.text: Performance work fails when it's one person's responsibility. It takes the whole team.

buildup.text: Designers choose image-heavy layouts. Product managers add third-party scripts. Code grows.

discovery.text: When everyone owns performance — design, product, engineering — regressions get caught early.

twist.text: Most performance regressions come from business decisions, not engineering mistakes.

climax.text: Building a performance culture means making speed a shared value, not just a tech metric.

punchline.text: Speed is a team value, not one person's job.

quiz.question: Where do most performance regressions originate?

hook.text: Marketing wants analytics. Sales wants chat widgets. Each adds a script tag to the page.

buildup.text: Third-party scripts run code you don't control on your users' browsers.

discovery.text: The average website loads 20+ third-party scripts, often adding 500 KB or more.

twist.text: A single slow third-party script can tank your Core Web Vitals, even if your code is perfect.

climax.text: Auditing and trimming third-party scripts is the most impactful and most political performance fix.

punchline.text: Other people's code is your performance problem.

quiz.question: Why are third-party scripts risky for performance?
options: You don't control their size or speed

hook.text: Lab tests show what could happen. Real User Monitoring shows what actually happened.

buildup.text: RUM collects performance data from every real page visit, across all devices and networks.

discovery.text: You see p50, p75, and p99 latencies — revealing how the slowest users actually experience your site.

twist.text: The p99 is often 10x slower than the median. The worst experience matters most.

climax.text: RUM turns performance from a guess into a science with real data from real users.

punchline.text: Real users show you what tests can't.

quiz.question: What does RUM stand for?

hook.text: Every byte transferred burns energy. The internet produces roughly 4% of global emissions.

buildup.text: Lighter pages mean less data transferred, fewer server cycles, and lower carbon footprints.

discovery.text: A fast website is an efficient website. Performance optimization is accidentally environmental.

twist.text: Dark mode saves energy on OLED screens. Design choices directly impact power consumption.

climax.text: Sustainable web design and performance optimization share the same goal: do more with less.

punchline.text: Fast pages are green pages.

quiz.question: How does web performance relate to sustainability?

hook.text: New standards and technologies keep pushing what's possible for web performance.

buildup.text: HTTP/3 uses QUIC to reduce connection setup time. 103 Early Hints start loading before HTML.

discovery.text: Edge computing runs server logic closer to users, cutting latency to single-digit milliseconds.

twist.text: Despite better tools, the average web page keeps getting heavier every year.

climax.text: Technology alone won't fix performance. It takes discipline, measurement, and culture.

punchline.text: Better tools don't fix bad habits.

quiz.question: What does edge computing reduce?
options: Latency by running code closer to users
